lessons.title: Hash Table Concept
lessons.concept: A hash table stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to compute an index (bucket) for each key, enabling fast average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion. The hash function maps keys to indices in an underlying array.
lessons.formula: index = hash(key) mod capacity. Average-case search/insert/delete: O(1). Worst-case can degrade (e.g., many collisions) to O(n) depending on implementation.
lessons.worked_example: Keys 15, 22 with capacity 10 and hash(k)=k: indices 5 and 2. Looking up key 15 computes index 5 and checks that bucket.
mistakes: Assuming hash tables always guarantee O(1) in worst case
Believing order of elements is preserved like an array/list
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Collisions and Resolution
lessons.concept: A collision occurs when different keys hash to the same index. Common resolution strategies include chaining (store multiple entries in a list/structure per bucket) and open addressing (probe for another slot, e.g., linear/quadratic probing, double hashing).
lessons.formula: Chaining: bucket[i] holds a collection of entries. Open addressing: try index, index+1, ... (linear) until empty slot found (with care for deletion).
lessons.worked_example: Capacity 10, keys 12 and 22 both hash to 2. With chaining, bucket 2 stores both entries. With linear probing, 22 may go to next available slot after 2.
mistakes: Forgetting that probing sequences must be handled correctly on search/delete
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Load Factor and Applications
lessons.concept: Load factor (entries/capacity) indicates how full a hash table is. High load factors increase collision likelihood and can degrade performance; resizing/rehashing is used to maintain efficiency. Hash tables power dictionaries/maps, sets, frequency counting, and fast membership checks.
lessons.formula: Load factor α = n / m (n entries, m buckets). Many implementations resize when α exceeds a threshold.
lessons.worked_example: Counting word frequencies: for each word, increment map[word]. Average O(1) per update makes this efficient for large inputs.
mistakes: Assuming unlimited capacity without resizing cost considerations
Using mutable objects incorrectly as keys in languages where hash/equality semantics matter
Expecting sorted iteration without additional structures

questions.explanation: Resizing and rehashing redistribute entries into a larger table, helping keep load factor low and operations efficient on average.
